Synapser is a wrapper around the Python client.  Due to this, there are some complexities in installing the package.  Please follow this guide.

## Prerequisites

- R 4.2.0 or later (R 4.1.x is not supported: it is the last Windows R with 32-bit multiarch, and reticulate 1.44.0 or later does not build for 32-bit Windows)
- reticulate 1.44.0 or later (earlier versions are incompatible with uv 0.8.0 and later, and fail with `could not find a Python environment for /`)

When synapser is loaded, it declares its Python requirement (`synapseclient[pandas]`, pinned to the version synapser wraps) via `reticulate::py_require()`. If reticulate does not find another Python configured on your machine, it uses [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) to download a compatible Python and the Synapse Python client into a managed environment, so you **DO NOT** need to install Python yourself. synapser supports Python 3.10 to 3.14 and does not request a specific one, so reticulate picks its own default: two minor versions behind the newest stable release (Python 3.12 as of reticulate 1.46.0). Run `reticulate::py_config()` to see which version you got. The first load may take a minute; later loads reuse the cached environment.

By default, reticulate only uses this managed environment when no other Python takes precedence in its [Order of Discovery](https://rstudio.github.io/reticulate/articles/versions.html#order-of-discovery). In particular, synapser will use a different Python if any of the following apply:

- The `RETICULATE_PYTHON` or `RETICULATE_PYTHON_ENV` environment variable is set (this includes selecting a Python interpreter in RStudio's Project or Global Options).
- A Python virtual environment is activated (`VIRTUAL_ENV` is set), or your working directory contains a `.venv`, `venv`, or similar virtual environment.
- A virtual environment named `r-reticulate` exists (for example, `~/.virtualenvs/r-reticulate`, created by earlier versions of these instructions).

In those cases synapser installs the Synapse Python client into that Python, which must be version 3.10 to 3.14. To use the managed environment instead, remove the conflicting setting, e.g. `reticulate::virtualenv_remove("r-reticulate")`, and restart R. You can check which Python synapser is using with `reticulate::py_config()`.

## Install SynapseR from GitHub

The synapser source code is on GitHub at [Sage-Bionetworks/synapser](https://github.com/Sage-Bionetworks/synapser). Installing from GitHub is useful if you want to try changes that have not been released yet, or to install an older release: the [Sage Bionetworks R-universe](https://sage-bionetworks.r-universe.dev) repository only serves the current version. For everyday use, install from R-universe as shown in [Install from R](#install-from-r) below.

1. **Install the `remotes` package** if you don't already have it:
   ```r
   if (!require("remotes", quietly = TRUE)) {
     install.packages("remotes")
   }
   ```

2. **Install synapser from GitHub.** Without a `ref`, this installs the default branch, `develop`, which contains the latest development changes:
   ```r
   remotes::install_github("Sage-Bionetworks/synapser")
   ```

3. **Optionally, install a specific branch or release** by passing `ref`:
   ```r
   # The latest release
   remotes::install_github("Sage-Bionetworks/synapser", ref = "master")

   # A specific release, by its tag (for example, 2.1.5)
   remotes::install_github("Sage-Bionetworks/synapser", ref = "2.1.5")
   ```

4. **Restart R, then load synapser** to confirm the installation:
   ```r
   library(synapser)
   packageVersion("synapser")
   ```

## Install R

1. Install R v4.2.0 or later
    a. Download links
        i. For macOS users, you can select a mirror and download R [here](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/macosx/)
        ii. For Windows and Linux users, you can select a mirror and download R [here](https://cran.r-project.org/mirrors.html)
    NOTE: R 4.1.x and earlier are not supported. On Windows, R 4.1.x is the last release with 32-bit multiarch, which the required version of reticulate cannot build for.
1. Install [RStudio Desktop](https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/#rstudio-ide-oss-downloads)
1. For Windows users, if you intend to run the project from outside [RStudio Desktop](https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/#rstudio-ide-oss-downloads)
(for example: VS Code or Terminal) the only additional step is to add R to system path: `C:\Program Files\R\R-4.2.0\bin\R.exe`

## Install from RStudio

- This guide assumes you have R and RStudio Desktop installed as described above.
- This guide will presume most users want to install and work with Synapse from RStudio Desktop.

You do not need to select a Python interpreter: by default synapser uses its managed environment (see [Prerequisites](#prerequisites)).
Only follow the steps below if you want synapser to use a specific Python 3.10 to 3.14 interpreter. Selecting one in RStudio sets
`RETICULATE_PYTHON`, which takes precedence over the managed environment.

1. Select your project's desired Python interpreter

  ![Python interpreter selection dialog](synapser_select_py.png){#id .class width=600 height=400px}

  ![Selected reticulate virtual environment in RStudio](synapser_final.png){#id .class width=600 height=400px}

  In the example above, we can see that a Python environment installed from the official Python installer and NOT the Python
version that shipped on macOS - is selected. The version you select must be Python 3.10 to 3.14.


## Install from R

### Step-by-Step Installation

You do not need to install Python first: synapser downloads a compatible Python and the Synapse Python client into a managed environment the first time it is loaded (see [Prerequisites](#prerequisites)).

1. **Remove any `r-reticulate` virtual environment left over from earlier versions of these instructions**, so it does not take precedence over the managed environment:
   ```r
   reticulate::virtualenv_remove(envname = "r-reticulate")
   ```

2. **If you previously pinned `rjson` or `reticulate` for synapser 2.x**, undo those pins.
   synapser 3.0.0 works with current versions of both, and it requires reticulate 1.44.0
   or later — `reticulate` 1.28 will break it:
   ```r
   install.packages(c("rjson", "reticulate"))
   packageVersion("reticulate")  # must be >= 1.44.0
   ```

3. **Install synapser** from the Sage Bionetworks R-universe repository:
   ```r
   install.packages("synapser", repos = c("https://sage-bionetworks.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
   ```

   **Installing from source:**
   ```r
   remotes::install_local(path = ".", upgrade = "never")
   ```

4. **Restart R, then load synapser.** The first load sets up the managed Python environment, which may take a minute:
   ```r
   library(synapser)
   reticulate::py_config()  # shows which Python synapser is using
   ```

### Using a Python environment you manage

If you would rather use your own Python 3.10 to 3.14 environment, select it before loading synapser, for example with `RETICULATE_PYTHON` or:
```r
reticulate::use_virtualenv("my-python-env", required = TRUE)
library(synapser)
```
synapser then installs the Synapse Python client into that environment the first time it loads.

## Troubleshooting

- If you get an error that it cannot find the synapseclient module, reticulate is using a different Python than you expect. Run `reticulate::py_config()` to see which one. To use synapser's managed environment instead, clear the interpreter selected under Tools > Project Options (or Global Options) > Python in [RStudio Desktop](https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/#rstudio-ide-oss-downloads), unset `RETICULATE_PYTHON`, and restart R.
- If you have already tried building the project with an older version of Python, remove `~/.virtualenvs/r-reticulate` (`reticulate::virtualenv_remove("r-reticulate")`) and restart R.
- If you halt the build process, a lock file might be left behind, which will need to be manually deleted (`$HOME\AppData\Local\R\win-library\4.2\00LOCK-synapser`)
- macOS ships with Python by default - Python 3.8 or Python 3.9.6 at the location `/usr/bin/python`3 - but it doesn't work well.
- If you're intending to run the project from terminal or VSCode on Windows and forgot to add python to path, it can be added manually using system environment variables: `C:\Users\USER\AppData\Local\Programs\Python\Python310\`

# (Optional) Managing Python 

This step is optional, but recommended if you plan to use multiple Python versions or want full control over your Python environment. Most synapser users do **not** need pyenv unless they have special requirements.
## Option 1: Using pyenv (Recommended)

We strongly recommend using `pyenv` to manage Python versions, as it provides better compatibility and easier version switching. This is especially important for synapser, which requires Python 3.10-3.14.

Find more information about `pyenv` [here](https://github.com/pyenv/pyenv?tab=readme-ov-file#installation)

### Install pyenv

**For macOS:**
```bash
# Using Homebrew (recommended)
brew install pyenv

# Or using the automatic installer
curl https://pyenv.run | bash
```

**For Linux (including Ubuntu/Amazon Linux):**
```bash
# Install dependencies first
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y make build-essential libssl-dev zlib1g-dev \
libbz2-dev libreadline-dev libsqlite3-dev wget curl llvm libncurses5-dev \
libncursesw5-dev xz-utils tk-dev libffi-dev liblzma-dev python3-openssl git

# Install pyenv
curl https://pyenv.run | bash
```

**For Amazon Linux 2/RHEL/CentOS:**
```bash
# Install dependencies first
sudo yum groupinstall -y "Development Tools"
sudo yum install -y zlib-devel bzip2-devel readline-devel sqlite-devel libffi-devel \
openssl-devel xz-devel libffi-devel

# Install pyenv
curl https://pyenv.run | bash
```

### Configure pyenv

To make pyenv available permanently, you need to add it to your shell configuration file. The temporary `export` command only works for the current session.

**Step 1: Determine your shell**
```bash
echo $SHELL
# Common outputs:
# /bin/bash  -> use ~/.bashrc or ~/.bash_profile
# /bin/zsh   -> use ~/.zshrc
```

**Step 2: Add pyenv to your shell configuration file**

**For bash users:**
```bash
# Add to ~/.bashrc (Linux) or ~/.bash_profile (macOS)
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.pyenv/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc
echo 'eval "$(pyenv init --path)"' >> ~/.bashrc
echo 'eval "$(pyenv init -)"' >> ~/.bashrc

# For macOS bash users, also add to ~/.bash_profile
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.pyenv/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.bash_profile
echo 'eval "$(pyenv init --path)"' >> ~/.bash_profile
echo 'eval "$(pyenv init -)"' >> ~/.bash_profile
```

**For zsh users:**
```bash
# Add to ~/.zshrc
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.pyenv/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc
echo 'eval "$(pyenv init --path)"' >> ~/.zshrc
echo 'eval "$(pyenv init -)"' >> ~/.zshrc
```

**Alternative: Manual editing**
You can also manually edit the configuration file:
```bash
# For bash
nano ~/.bashrc    # or ~/.bash_profile on macOS

# For zsh  
nano ~/.zshrc
```

Then add these lines to the file:
```bash
export PATH="$HOME/.pyenv/bin:$PATH"
eval "$(pyenv init --path)"
eval "$(pyenv init -)"
```

**Step 3: Apply the changes**
```bash
# Reload your shell configuration
source ~/.bashrc    # for bash on Linux
source ~/.bash_profile  # for bash on macOS
source ~/.zshrc     # for zsh

# OR restart your terminal
```

**Step 4: Verify pyenv is working**
```bash
pyenv --version
which pyenv  # Should show /home/username/.pyenv/bin/pyenv
```

### Install and set Python 3.10

```bash
# List available Python versions
pyenv install --list | grep " 3\.10"

# Install Python 3.10 (recommended version)
pyenv install 3.10

# Set as global default (optional)
pyenv global 3.10

# Or set as local for your project directory
cd /path/to/your/project
pyenv local 3.10

# Verify installation
python --version  # Should show Python 3.10
pyenv version
```

## Option 2: Official Python Installer (Alternative)

If you prefer not to use pyenv, you can install Python from the official installers:

1. Install Python from one of the official [Python installers](https://www.python.org/downloads/) - version 3.10 to 3.14 and remove other versions of Python except for the one that ships with macOS located in `usr/bin/python` (note for windows: make sure to add Python to path if you're planning on running the project from outside RStudio, for example from terminal). TIP: You can verify which version you have with....

    ```
    % which -a python3
    /usr/bin/python3		# <- Default Python shipped with macOS

    % which -a python3
    /usr/local/bin/python3	# <- Official Python installer (3.11.1 for me)
    /usr/bin/python3		# <- Default Python shipped with macOS
    ```

    macOS ships with Python by default - Python 3.8 or Python 3.9.6 at the location /usr/bin/python3 - but it doesn't work well.

    Only the official installer versions work. Seriously. Please do yourself a favor and avoid having a very long, sad day because you insisted on using the version that shipped with macOS by default.
